title: Sorting via Subarray Reversals
approach_explanation: The problem asks whether an array of size $n$ can be sorted in non-decreasing order by repeatedly reversing subarrays of length at most $k$. If the array is already sorted, the answer is trivially "YES". If the array is not sorted, we can always reverse any adjacent pair of elements if $k \\ge 2$. By repeatedly reversing adjacent pairs (similar to Bubble Sort), we can generate any permutation of the array. Thus, if $k \\ge 2$, any unsorted array can be sorted. The only case where we cannot sort an unsorted array is when $k = 1$, because a subarray of length $1$ cannot be reversed to change any order.

code_breakdown.section_title: Test Case Loop and Input Reading
code_breakdown.explanation: Reads the number of test cases $t$, and for each test case reads $n$ (number of elements) and $k$ (maximum reverse length).
Iterates through the array elements, keeping track of the previous element to verify if the entire array is already sorted in non-decreasing order.
Calls the `solve` function which outputs "YES" if the array is already sorted or if $k \\ge 2$, and "NO" if the array is not sorted and $k = 1$.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: For each test case, we iterate through the array of size $n$ once to check if it is sorted. With $t$ test cases, the total time complexity is $O(\\sum n)$, which is bounded by $O(t \\cdot \\max(n))$ i.e., $100 \\times 100 = 10^4$ operations, easily fitting well within the 1-second time limit.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: The algorithm processes inputs on-the-fly without storing the array elements in any secondary data structures like vectors or arrays, using only a constant number of scalar variables.

strengths: Optimal $O(n)$ time complexity and $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
